summary: Philip Rathle opens a round table session at the AI Engineer World's Fair focused on challenges of moving GenAI prototypes to production, organized around the concept of stakes. He establishes two ground rules: collaborative problem-solving and Chatham House rules for confidentiality. Rathle observes the familiar pattern — prototypes are easy to build but production raises the bar — and presents a progression of technical unlocks: first RAG with vectors, then knowledge graphs and graph RAG, while noting the world tends to move in S-curves rather than hockey sticks. He frames a spectrum of application stakes. Low-stakes problems like summarizing a bedtime story tolerate imprecision. High-stakes problems involve dollar impact, brand and reputational damage, health and human safety, regulatory fines, and bias. A middle zone exists where human-in-the-loop mitigations help, corresponding to a co-pilot model versus a fully autonomous pilot. Higher stakes amplify familiar challenges: enterprise domain knowledge, hallucinations, and error tolerance, illustrated with a Boeing 737 Max 9 metaphor about acceptable error rates. Rathle contrasts vector-based representations — statistical, proximity-based, right-brain-like, sometimes wrong without explanation — with knowledge graphs — structured, human-understandable, machine-reasonable, left-brain-like. Combined with LLMs, knowledge graphs bring facts, reasoning, discernment, and long-term memory, creating a better-together dynamic. The session then turns to audience learnings across two rounds. Early contributors emphasize understanding stakes and scope upfront, matching deterministic tools to deterministic questions while reserving LLMs for tasks they excel at, asking LLMs to write code rather than directly solve problems, anticipating that users may default to keyword search, killing weak projects early, making cost-to-quality and cost-to-speed trade-offs deliberately, and navigating the tension between waiting for better base models versus building now, exemplified by Bloomberg fine-tuning Llama 2 only to find base Llama 3 outperforming it. Later contributors add critical lessons: avoid premature optimization by validating with the best available large model before fine-tuning down, set a ceiling on implementation time since new models may obsolete long projects, build eval pipelines from day zero with the right data, do not hide AI from end users — use UI cues like slow generation, specific colors, and icons to signal vigilance, and for regulated industries use human-in-the-loop with transparent input sourcing, side-by-side verification, and multi-option outputs rather than deterministic single answers. A behavioral health practitioner describes showing source documentation alongside AI-generated summaries paragraph by paragraph, enabling clinician editing, and using thumbs-up/down feedback plus clinical evaluation as eval stages. A personal loan recommendation use case illustrates giving three explained options instead of a single deterministic recommendation to satisfy regulators.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Prototypes are easy; production raises the bar significantly, especially as stakes increase
A stakes spectrum — from low (text summarization) to high (health, safety, regulation, financial impact) — determines required accuracy and technical approach
RAG with vectors is a first unlock; knowledge graphs and graph RAG provide a second unlock for higher-stakes use cases requiring structured reasoning
Use deterministic tools for deterministic questions; reserve LLMs for what they excel at such as query formulation and audience-aware text modulation
Avoid premature optimization: validate product viability with the best large model first, then fine-tune down — starting small risks wrongly concluding a task is impossible
Build eval pipelines from day zero and ensure you have the right data to evaluate whether prompt changes improve or degrade performance
Do not hide AI from end users: use UI cues (slow generation, colors, icons) to encourage vigilance and provide tools for answer validation
For regulated industries, maintain human-in-the-loop with transparent input sourcing, side-by-side verification, and multi-option outputs rather than deterministic single answers
Set a ceiling on implementation time — long projects risk obsolescence as new base models arrive
Kill weak projects early during experimentation and focus effort on the few that can realistically reach production

sections.title: Opening and round table setup
sections.summary: Philip introduces the round table format, ground rules (collaboration and Chatham House rules), and the goal of learning from each other about getting to production challenges around stakes.

sections.title: Stakes spectrum and technical unlocks
sections.summary: Rathle presents the hockey-stick to S-curve pattern, RAG with vectors as a first unlock and knowledge graphs and graph RAG as a second unlock. He introduces a stakes spectrum from low (text summarization) to high (dollar impact, brand, health, safety, regulation, bias), and the pilot vs co-pilot distinction tied to stakes.

sections.title: Vector vs knowledge graph representations
sections.summary: Using an apple example, Rathle contrasts vector representations (statistical, proximity-based, right-brain-like) with knowledge graphs (structured, human-understandable, machine-reasonable, left-brain-like). Combined with LLMs, knowledge graphs bring facts, reasoning, discernment, and long-term memory for a better-together dynamic.

sections.title: Audience learnings: scoping, cost, and model selection
sections.summary: Audience members share lessons: understand stakes and scope upfront, use deterministic tools for deterministic questions while reserving LLMs for query formulation and text modulation, ask LLMs to write code rather than solve directly, anticipate users defaulting to keyword search, kill weak projects early, manage cost-to-quality and cost-to-speed trade-offs, and navigate the tension between waiting for better base models versus building now, illustrated by Bloomberg's Llama 2 fine-tuning being outperformed by base Llama 3.

sections.title: Audience learnings: optimization, eval, transparency, and regulation
sections.summary: Audience contributors add: set a ceiling on implementation time since long projects may be obsoleted by new models; avoid premature optimization by validating with large models first before fine-tuning down; build eval pipelines from day zero with the right data; do not hide AI from users — use UI cues like slow generation, colors, and icons to encourage vigilance and provide validation tools. For regulated industries like behavioral health, maintain human-in-the-loop with transparent input sourcing and side-by-side summaries editable paragraph by paragraph, using user feedback and clinical evaluation as eval stages. For personal loan recommendations in regulated contexts, give multiple explained options rather than a single deterministic answer. The session closes with encouragement to continue discussion at lunch.

demonstrations: Apple example contrasting multi-dimensional human conceptualization with vector representation via cosine similarity
Boeing 737 Max 9 metaphor for error tolerance thresholds in high-stakes applications
Behavioral health use case: side-by-side source documentation and AI-generated summaries with paragraph-level clinician editing capability
Personal loan recommendation: three explained options instead of a single deterministic answer to satisfy regulators
limitations: Vector-based RAG insufficient for highest-stakes use cases requiring structured reasoning
LLMs inherently non-deterministic, not suited for questions requiring exact deterministic answers
Fine-tuning effort may be obsoleted by next-generation base models
User adoption of semantic search over keyword search is not guaranteed
Long implementation timelines risk being thrown away as new models arrive
Premature optimization with small fine-tuned models can incorrectly conclude tasks aren't possible
Lack of eval data blocks assessment of whether prompt changes improve or degrade performance
quantitativeClaims: Bloomberg fine-tuned Llama 2 for financial data, then base Llama 3 outperformed the fine-tuned model
0.001% error rate referenced as insufficient for high-stakes applications like aviation
